newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan says may nix aid to N.Korea over drug case.
newsitem.headline: Japan says may nix aid to N.Korea over drug case.

text.p: Japan's top government spokesman said on Tuesday Japan may not give food aid to North Korea because of a big drug seizure aboard a North Korean freighter and suspicions over kidnapped Japanese nationals.

"North Korea is that kind of country and it is hard to believe that civilians were behind the drug case," Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama said in the first government reaction to the huge drug haul last week.

"If the ship did not truly call on any other port before coming to Japan, then we must suspect something," Kajiyama told a news conference. "This, along with the suspected kidnappings, makes it even more difficult to extend aid."
Last week, Japanese police arrested a captain of a North Korean freighter and two pro-Pyongyang Korean residents in Japan on suspicion of smuggling a huge cache of stimulants.
Investigators found 70 kg (154 lb) of amphetamines with a street value estimated at 11.9 billion yen ($95 million) in cargo from the 1,499-tonne freighter Ji Song-2.
The drugs were found in containers labelled honey in cargo the ship offloaded at the tiny port of Hososhima on the Pacific coast of the southern main island of Kyushu.
The ship left North Korea's Nanpo port on April 5 and arrived in Japan three days later. It later steamed to the western Japan port of Shimonoseki and is being held there.

Kajiyama also said Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto may tell U.S. President Bill Clinton of his concerns over extending food aid to North Korea because of the drug smuggling case and suspicions that North Korean agents kidnapped Japanese nationals in the late 1970s and 1980s.
Hashimoto meets Clinton in Washington at the weekend.
"The United States has been sensitive about drugs and I am sure that they will understand our point," Kajiyama said.
U.S. officials have repeatedly asked Japan to join the United States and South Korea in providing food aid to famine-stricken North Korea.

Last month, Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said the government will hold up a decision on the food aid because of public anger over allegations that North Korea kidnapped and spirited away several Japanese citizens to Pyongyang.
Also on Tuesday, Japanese newspapers reported that one of 17 crewmembers aboard the North Korean freighter may be a North Korean spy.

Quoting police sources, the dailies Tokyo Shimbun and Sankei Shimbun said Japanese investigators believe the North Korean belonged to an intelligence unit within North Korea's military or ruling Korea Workers' (communist) Party.
The dailies said intelligence equipment including a table of random secret codes was also found on the North Korean-registered Ji Song-2.
A spokesman for Miyazaki Prefectural Police, in charge of the investigation, declined to comment on the reports. In his news conference, Kajiyama did not talk about the reports of the suspected spy.
The dailies said Japanese authorities were investigating whether the Pyongyang government was involved in what could be the biggest ever drug smuggling case involving North Koreans.
Japanese intelligence sources said on Monday that they believe the cash-strapped North Korean government may have been behind the drug smuggling operation.
They said North Korea, gripped by famine after two consecutive years of flooding, may have been cornered into taking illegal steps to earn foreign exchange.
